{#t9hn} # Discussion

{#fb2k} ⟨待采纳·删除·张教授⟩ In the present analysis, we explored the optimal treatment for LS-SCLC with bulky tumor. Our results demonstrated that compared to sequential TRT combined with cisplatin and intravenous etoposide, concurrent TRT combined with cisplatin and oral etoposide yielded more favorable PFS and OS with acceptable treatment-related toxicity among patients who had completed 3-4 cycles of induction chemotherapy and achieved a remission. Results from multivariate analysis also confirmed the benefit of concurrent chemoradiotherapy after induction chemotherapy in PFS and OS. Our results provided a more efficient treatment strategy for LS-SCLC with bulky tumor.

{#n7qu} ⟨待采纳·删除⟩ Previous studies suggested that early delivery of TRT seemed to be related to long-term survival [5, 6, 10, 12–14]. But a meta-analysis indicated that only patients who completed full doses of chemotherapy could benefit from early TRT [8]. One possible explanation for the advantage of administering early TRT was that it might eliminate chemotherapy-resistant tumor cells which always devoted to disseminate systemically and treatment failure [6]. Nevertheless, some limitations of early TRT should be taken into consideration. On one hand, since the preparation before radiotherapy was complicated, the initiation of TRT in the first cycle chemotherapy may delay, extending treatment time. On the other hand, unlike previous studies, all patients enrolled in current analysis had large tumor burden which required large radiation target volumes. Induction chemotherapy contributed to tumor shrinkage and significant reduction of radiation planning, decreasing toxicity in normal tissue [15, 16]. Considering this study included LS-SCLC patients with large tumor burden, induction chemotherapy was performed before TRT.

{#uxld} # Introduction

{#ayr5} The concurrent thoracic radiotherapy (TRT) combined with chemotherapy has been proved to improve overall survival (OS) and considered to be the standard treatment for limited-stage small-cell lung cancer (LS-SCLC) [1–3]. In the regimen of platinum chemotherapy concurrent with TRT, a significant higher 5-year survival was observed when chest radiotherapy was started within 30 days after the start of chemotherapy [4–7]. Other studies failed to show a survival advantage of early TRT with chemotherapy for LS-SCLC [8, 9]. In a Korean study of LS-SCLC, TRT starting in the third cycle of chemotherapy was not inferior to early TRT and had a more favorable profile with regard to neutropenic fever . However, patients with LS-SCLC always had bulky tumors that would require large radiation target volume with concomitant increase in acute or chronic toxicity. Chemoradiotherapy might be interrupted because of intolerance in most patients, thus therapeutic effect was affected. Compared with sequential late radiation therapy, early radiation therapy with poor implementation of chemotherapy did not improve the survival [10]. Therefore, 3-4 cycles of induction chemotherapy before TRT for LS-SCLC with bulky tumor was often performed in clinic, which also made up time for preparing TRT.

ops.markdown: Previous studies have suggested that early delivery of TRT is associated with improved long-term survival [5, 6, 10, 12–14]. However, a meta-analysis indicated that only patients who received full doses of chemotherapy could benefit from early TRT [8]. One plausible explanation for the advantage of early TRT is that it may eradicate chemotherapy-resistant tumor cells, which are prone to systemic dissemination and subsequent treatment failure [6]. Nevertheless, several limitations of early TRT should also be taken into consideration. On the one hand, because the preparation for radiotherapy is complex, initiating TRT during the first cycle of chemotherapy may be delayed, thereby prolonging the overall treatment time. On the other hand, unlike previous studies, all patients enrolled in the present analysis had a large tumor burden that necessitated large radiation target volumes. Induction chemotherapy contributed to tumor shrinkage and a substantial reduction in the radiation planning volume, thus decreasing toxicity to normal tissue [15, 16]. Given that this study included LS-SCLC patients with a large tumor burden, induction chemotherapy was therefore delivered before TRT. In a meta-analysis of seven randomized trials, Pijls-Johannesma et al. found that overall survival at 2 or 5 years was not significantly different between early and late chest radiotherapy, whereas in the trials that used platinum-based chemotherapy concurrently with chest radiotherapy, 2-year survival (HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.57-0.94; P=0.01) and 5-year survival (HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.45-0.93; P=0.02) were significantly higher when chest radiotherapy was started within 30 days after the start of chemotherapy [@c:c08fbf21].
